questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the x-Intercepts of an Ellipse By Completing the Square
questions.problem: Calculate the points where the ellipse  $9{x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}-36x+16y=-16$ intercepts the $x$-axis.
questions.worked_solution:
To calculate the $x$-intercepts, we need to substitute $y=0$ into the equation of the ellipse and solve the resulting equation for $x.$ We do this and solve the resulting equation by completing the square:

$$
\begin{aligned}9{x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}-36x+16y & =-16 \\ 9{x}^{2}+4(0)^{2}-36x+16(0) & =-16 \\ 9{x}^{2}-36x & =-16 \\ {x}^{2}-4x & =-\frac{16}{9} \\ (x-2)^{2}-{2}^{2} & =-\frac{16}{9} \\ (x-2)^{2} & =-\frac{16}{9}+4 \\ (x-2)^{2} & =-\frac{16}{9}+\frac{36}{9} \\ (x-2)^{2} & =\frac{20}{9} \\ x-2 & =\pm \frac{2\sqrt{5}}{3} \\ x & =2\pm \frac{2\sqrt{5}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the ellipse intercepts the $x$-axis at $(2-\frac{2\sqrt{5}}{3},0)$ and $(2+\frac{2\sqrt{5}}{3},0).$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the y-Intercepts of an Ellipse
questions.problem: Calculate the points where the ellipse $\frac{(x+1)^{2}}{5}+\frac{(y-1)^{2}}{10}=1$ intercepts the $y$-axis.
questions.worked_solution:
To calculate the $y$-intercept, we need to substitute $x=0$ in the equation of the ellipse and solve the resulting equation for $y.$ Doing this, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{(x+1)^{2}}{5}+\frac{(y-1)^{2}}{10} & =1 \\ \frac{(0+1)^{2}}{5}+\frac{(y-1)^{2}}{10} & =1 \\ \frac{1}{5}+\frac{(y-1)^{2}}{10} & =1 \\ 2+(y-1)^{2} & =10 \\ (y-1)^{2} & =8 \\ y-1 & =\pm 2\sqrt{2} \\ y & =1\pm 2\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the ellipse intercepts the $y$-axis at the points $(0,1-2\sqrt{2})$ and $(0,1+2\sqrt{2}).$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the x-Intercepts of an Ellipse By Completing the Square
questions.problem: Calculate the points where the ellipse ${x}^{2}+9{y}^{2}+4x+54y+76=0$ intercepts the $x$-axis.
questions.worked_solution:
To calculate the $x$-intercepts, we need to substitute $y=0$ into the equation of the ellipse and solve the resulting equation for $x.$ We do this and solve the resulting equation by completing the square:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+9{y}^{2}+4x+54y+76 & =0 \\ {x}^{2}+9\cdot {0}^{2}+4x+54\cdot 0+76 & =0 \\ {x}^{2}+4x+76 & =0 \\ (x+2)^{2}-4+76 & =0 \\ (x+2)^{2}+72 & =0 \\ (x+2)^{2} & =-72.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $(x+2)^{2}\ge 0$, there is no $x$ such that $(x+2)^{2}=-72.$ Therefore, the ellipse has no $x$-intercepts, meaning that it does not intercept the $x$-axis at any point.

questions.problem:
Calculate the point where the ellipse ${x}^{2}+6{y}^{2}+2x-12\sqrt{3}y+18=0$ intercepts the $y$-axis.

The $y$-intercept is $($

,

questions.worked_solution:
To calculate the $y$-intercepts, we need to substitute $x=0$ in the equation of the ellipse and try to solve the resulting equation for $y.$ We do this and solve the resulting equation by completing the square:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+6{y}^{2}+2x-12\sqrt{3}y+18 & =0 \\ (0)^{2}+6{y}^{2}+2(0)-12\sqrt{3}y+18 & =0 \\ 6{y}^{2}-12\sqrt{3}y+18 & =0 \\ 6[{y}^{2}-2\sqrt{3}y]+18 & =0 \\ 6[(y-\sqrt{3})^{2}-3]+18 & =0 \\ 6(y-\sqrt{3})^{2}-18+18 & =0 \\ 6(y-\sqrt{3})^{2} & =0 \\ y-\sqrt{3} & =0 \\ y & =\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the ellipse intercepts the $y$-axis at the point $(0,\sqrt{3}).$

questions.problem:
From **top to bottom**, the ellipse $\frac{(x-8)^{2}}{100}+\frac{(y+1)^{2}}{9}=1$ intercepts the $y$-axis at the points $A$ and $B.$ Find the coordinates of these points.

$A($
{{field-1}}
$,\frac{4}{5})\,$

and 

$\,B($
{{field-2}}$,$
{{field-3}}
$)$
questions.worked_solution:
To calculate the $y$-intercept, we need to substitute $x=0$ in the equation of the ellipse and solve the resulting equation for $y.$ Doing this, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{(x-8)^{2}}{100}+\frac{(y+1)^{2}}{9} & =1 \\ \frac{(0-8)^{2}}{100}+\frac{(y+1)^{2}}{9} & =1 \\ \frac{64}{100}+\frac{(y+1)^{2}}{9} & =1 \\ 144+25(y+1)^{2} & =225 \\ 25(y+1)^{2} & =81 \\ (y+1)^{2} & =\frac{81}{25} \\ y+1 & =\pm \frac{9}{5} \\ y & =-1\pm \frac{9}{5} \\ y & =-\frac{14}{5},\frac{4}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, from top to bottom, the $y$-intercepts are

$$
A(0,\frac{4}{5})\,\text{and}\,B(0,-\frac{14}{5}).
$$
